sections.heading: Overview
sections.wikitext:
[[File:Jackie Wilson 1961.jpg|thumb|upright|Jackie Wilson in 1961|left]]

The backing track was recorded on July 6, 1967 at [[Columbia Records|Columbia's]] studios in Chicago. Produced by [[Carl Davis (record producer)|Carl Davis]], the session, arranged by [[Sonny Sanders]], featured bassist [[James Jamerson]], drummer [[Richard "Pistol" Allen]], guitarist [[Robert White (guitarist)|Robert White]], and keyboardist [[Johnny Griffith (musician)|Johnny Griffith]]; these four musicians were all members of the [[Motown Records]] house band [[The Funk Brothers]] who often moonlighted on sessions for Davis to augment the wages paid by Motown.<ref name=RussAndGary>{{cite web |url=https://strathdee.wordpress.com/2010/05/08/jackie-wilson/ |title=Jackie Wilson |website=Russ & Gary's "The Best Years of Music"|date=May 9, 2010 }}</ref>{{Better source needed|reason=source is a blog|date=April 2019}}

According to Carl Davis, the Funk Brothers "used to come over on the weekends from Detroit. They'd load up in the van and come over to Chicago, and I would pay 'em double scale, and I'd pay 'em in cash."<ref name=RussAndGary /> Similarly, two members of Motown's house session singers [[The Andantes]], Jackie Hicks and Marlene Barrow, along with [[Pat Lewis]] (who was filling in for Andantes member Louvain Demps), performed on the session for "Higher and Higher".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://doo-wop.blogg.org/andantes-c26504834 |title=The Andantes |website=Doo Wop Blog}}</ref> 
Drummer [[Maurice White]] (better known as a singer for [[Earth, Wind & Fire]]) also played on the recording.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/talent/detail/155723/White_Maurice_instrumentalist_drums |title=Maurice White (instrumentalist : drums) |website=DAHR: Discography of American Historical Recordings}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.soulandjazzandfunk.com/interviews/3872-maurice-white-philosopher-and-truth-seeker-an-appreciation.html |title=MAURICE WHITE, PHILOSOPHER AND TRUTH SEEKER - AN APPRECIATION |website=Soul and Jazz and Funk.com |access-date=June 12, 2018 |archive-date=June 12, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612232706/http://www.soulandjazzandfunk.com/interviews/3872-maurice-white-philosopher-and-truth-seeker-an-appreciation.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Motown's [[Mike Terry (saxophonist)|Mike Terry]] played the baritone saxophone.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2008/dec/01/mike-terry-obituary|title = Obituary: Mike Terry| newspaper=The Guardian |date = December 2008 | last1=Williams | first1=Richard }}</ref>

The song was originally written by Chess Records' in-house writers and producers Carl Smith and Raynard Miner, and initially recorded by The Dells for the label, but not released. Another writer, Gary Jackson, made some changes to the song and pitched it to Davis at Brunswick. When the singer recorded his vocal track, Davis recalls, [[Jackie Wilson]] originally sang the song "like a soul ballad. I said that's totally wrong. You have to jump and go with the percussion... If he didn't want to sing it that way, I would put my voice on the record and sell millions." After hearing Davis' advice, Wilson cut the lead vocal for "Higher and Higher" in a single take.<ref>{{cite web|title=Jackie Wilson on Columbia Records |url=http://www.brunswickrecords.com/artists/jackiewilson.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090522124509/http://www.brunswickrecords.com/artists/jackiewilson.htm |archive-date=May 22, 2009 |url-status=dead |access-date=2009-06-30 |df=mdy }}</ref>

A publishing deal for the song was reached with Brunswick after Chess producer/A&R head, Billy Davis, intervened. Writing credits were agreed, with Smith, Miner, Jackson and Billy Davis all named. Later, Davis removed his credit, and BMI now lists the song as by the three other writers. The Dells' version appeared on their album, ''There Is'', for Chess subsidiary Cadet the same year.

The backing track was recorded on July 6, 1967 at Columbia's studios in Chicago. Produced by Carl Davis, the session, arranged by Sonny Sanders, featured bassist James Jamerson, drummer Richard "Pistol" Allen, guitarist Robert White, and keyboardist Johnny Griffith; these four musicians were all members of the Motown Records house band The Funk Brothers who often moonlighted on sessions for Davis to augment the wages paid by Motown.{{Better source needed|reason=source is a blog|date=April 2019}}

According to Carl Davis, the Funk Brothers "used to come over on the weekends from Detroit. They'd load up in the van and come over to Chicago, and I would pay 'em double scale, and I'd pay 'em in cash." Similarly, two members of Motown's house session singers The Andantes, Jackie Hicks and Marlene Barrow, along with Pat Lewis (who was filling in for Andantes member Louvain Demps), performed on the session for "Higher and Higher". 
Drummer Maurice White (better known as a singer for Earth, Wind & Fire) also played on the recording. Motown's Mike Terry played the baritone saxophone.

The song was originally written by Chess Records' in-house writers and producers Carl Smith and Raynard Miner, and initially recorded by The Dells for the label, but not released. Another writer, Gary Jackson, made some changes to the song and pitched it to Davis at Brunswick. When the singer recorded his vocal track, Davis recalls, Jackie Wilson originally sang the song "like a soul ballad. I said that's totally wrong. You have to jump and go with the percussion... If he didn't want to sing it that way, I would put my voice on the record and sell millions." After hearing Davis' advice, Wilson cut the lead vocal for "Higher and Higher" in a single take.

A publishing deal for the song was reached with Brunswick after Chess producer/A&R head, Billy Davis, intervened. Writing credits were agreed, with Smith, Miner, Jackson and Billy Davis all named. Later, Davis removed his credit, and BMI now lists the song as by the three other writers. The Dells' version appeared on their album, There Is, for Chess subsidiary Cadet the same year.

sections.heading: Certifications
Film and television
sections.wikitext: Wilson's original version and a cover version by singer [[Howard Huntsberry]] were both used in the 1989 comedy film ''[[Ghostbusters II]]'', with Huntsberry's version also appearing on [[Ghostbusters II (soundtrack)|the soundtrack]]. Wilson's original version was also used in the end credits of the films ''[[For Love or Money (1993 film)|For Love or Money]]'', ''[[The Bachelor (1999 film)|The Bachelor]]'', ''[[Disney's The Kid|The Kid]]'', ''[[Death to Smoochy]]'', and ''[[Date Night]]'', as well as the [[Stranger Things season 3|third season]] of the [[Netflix]] series ''[[Stranger Things]]'' (specifically the episode "[[Chapter Eight: The Battle of Starcourt]]").
sections.text: Wilson's original version and a cover version by singer Howard Huntsberry were both used in the 1989 comedy film Ghostbusters II, with Huntsberry's version also appearing on the soundtrack. Wilson's original version was also used in the end credits of the films For Love or Money, The Bachelor, The Kid, Death to Smoochy, and Date Night, as well as the third season of the Netflix series Stranger Things (specifically the episode "Chapter Eight: The Battle of Starcourt").

sections.heading: Politics
sections.wikitext: An instrumental version of the song was played for then-Vice President [[Joe Biden]] at both the [[2012 Democratic National Convention|2012]] and [[2016 Democratic National Convention|2016 Democratic National Conventions]] during his address to the delegates. The song was later played after Biden's first speech as President-elect during the [[2020 United States Presidential Election]] and again for his closing address on the opening night of the [[2024 Democratic National Convention]].
sections.text: An instrumental version of the song was played for then-Vice President Joe Biden at both the 2012 and 2016 Democratic National Conventions during his address to the delegates. The song was later played after Biden's first speech as President-elect during the 2020 United States Presidential Election and again for his closing address on the opening night of the 2024 Democratic National Convention.

3:28 (single edit) | label = [[A&M Records]] | writer = Billy Davis, Gary Jackson, Raynard Miner and Carl Smith | producer = [[David Anderle]] | prev_title = [[Mean to Me (1929 song)|Mean to Me]] | prev_year = 1975 | next_title = [[We're All Alone#Rita Coolidge version|We're All Alone]] | next_year = 1977 }} [[Rita Coolidge]] remade the song as "(Your Love Has Lifted Me) Higher and Higher" for her album ''[[Anytime...Anywhere]]'' (1977). Her version has a more moderate tempo than that of the uptempo original, and largely omits the chorus which is evidenced only in the background vocals sung under the repetition of the first verse with which she closes the song. Coolidge and her sister [[Priscilla Coolidge]] had sung background on a version of the song for a prospective album by Priscilla's husband [[Booker T. Jones]]; when that album was shelved, Coolidge asked him if she could cut the song using his arrangement. {{cite web |url=http://www.spencerleigh.demon.co.uk/Interview_Coolidge.htm |title=Country Music People 10/06 |access-date=May 4, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070222222209/http://www.spencerleigh.demon.co.uk/Interview_Coolidge.htm |archive-date=February 22, 2007 |url-status=dead }} Released as a single, Coolidge's version became her first major hit in nine years of recording: the track peaked at No. 2 on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100.{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.billboard.com/charts/hot-100/1977-09-10|title=The Hot 100 Chart|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] }} ''[[Cash Box]]'' ranked it at No. 1.{{cite web |url=http://cashboxmagazine.com/archives/70s_files/19770910.html |title=CASH BOX Top 100 Singles |access-date=2014-12-23 |df=mdy |archive-date=August 14, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120814104049/http://cashboxmagazine.com/archives/70s_files/19770910.html |url-status=dead }}{{cite web|author=Cash Box Magazine |url=http://cashboxmagazine.com/archives/70s_files/19770910.html |title=Cash Box Top 100 9/10/77 |date=September 10, 1977 |access-date=2014-07-17 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120814104049/http://cashboxmagazine.com/archives/70s_files/19770910.html |archive-date=August 14, 2012 }} "Higher and Higher" also reached No. 1 in Canada. Both the song and a subsequent release, "[[We're All Alone]]", earned Coolidge [[RIAA certification|gold record]]s for each selling a million copies. In the UK it was released as the follow-up single after "We're All Alone" which had reached No. 6, but it only achieved a peak of No. 48 there.{{cite web |title=(Your Love Has Lifted Me) Higher and Higher: Full Official Chart History |url=http://www.officialcharts.com/search/singles/(your%20love%20has%20lifted%20me)%20higher%20and%20higher/ |website=Official Charts|access-date=24 July 2017}}

Her version has a more moderate tempo than that of the uptempo original, and largely omits the chorus which is evidenced only in the background vocals sung under the repetition of the first verse with which she closes the song. Coolidge and her sister Priscilla Coolidge had sung background on a version of the song for a prospective album by Priscilla's husband Booker T. Jones; when that album was shelved, Coolidge asked him if she could cut the song using his arrangement. Released as a single, Coolidge's version became her first major hit in nine years of recording: the track peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100. Cash Box ranked it at No. 1. "Higher and Higher" also reached No. 1 in Canada. Both the song and a subsequent release, "We're All Alone", earned Coolidge gold records for each selling a million copies. In the UK it was released as the follow-up single after "We're All Alone" which had reached No. 6, but it only achieved a peak of No. 48 there.

sections.heading: Kevin Borg version
sections.wikitext: In 2008, [[Kevin Borg (singer)|Kevin Borg]] performed the song, still known as "Higher and Higher", and became the winner of season eight of Sweden's version of ''[[Idol (Sweden)|Idol]]''. The version charted in [[Sverigetopplistan|Sweden]], peaking at number twenty-nine.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://acharts.us/sweden_singles_top_60/2008/49 |title=Sweden Singles Top 60 (December 4, 2008) – Music Charts |website=αCharts |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111204160443/http://acharts.us/sweden_singles_top_60/2008/49 |archive-date=December 4, 2011 |url-status=live |df=mdy }}</ref>
sections.text: In 2008, Kevin Borg performed the song, still known as "Higher and Higher", and became the winner of season eight of Sweden's version of Idol. The version charted in Sweden, peaking at number twenty-nine.
